Case Study · Consumer Lending

Making great work possible on an impossible timeline.

Close enough to the craft to lead it — I reframed design from the program's blocker into the blueprint the build depended on, and we shipped all six features on deadline.

Design LeadershipStrategy Program RescueProduct DesignShipped ✓

Context

  • Consumer Lending's digital transformation hinged on a vendor to re-platform and inherit out-of-the-box capabilities.
  • The vendor failed enterprise security & compliance vetting — leaving ~9 months to build a new servicing platform from scratch.
  • All under active regulatory exposure — penalties severe enough to take Consumer Lending offline if not corrected by the deadline.
  • The partner org had never integrated design into delivery — and assumed it could run parallel to development.

Approach

  • Reframed design's role at the executive level: design decisions drive development — design is the blueprint, not the blocker.
  • Rebuilt stakeholder trust and taught partners how to fold design into delivery.
  • Prioritized ruthlessly to six mission-critical features.
  • Ran a stair-stepped, rolling delivery model to keep the team at full capacity to the deadline.

Outcome

  • All six member- and MSR-facing experiences designed and shipped — on our stringently governed, highly accessible design system.
  • Delivered on deadline despite the window: ~5 of 9 months lost to escalation, leaving ~3–4 months to design all six — then we supported dev through full delivery and launch.
  • New Member/MSR parity, visible status, and automation that cut manual error and call volume.
  • A repeatable design process and roadmap — the foundation for Phase 2.
Role: Design Director & Project Lead (also filling the lead/senior-designer role)  ·  Timeline: ~9-month program, ~3–4-month design window  ·  Team: me + a mid-level and a junior designer, with Product, Engineering, Business & Compliance  ·  Shipped ✓

Where this sat

At the center of Consumer Lending

Consumer Lending servicing spans what members do themselves and what member service reps (MSRs) do on their behalf — all on aging platforms, all under a regulatory microscope. A miss here isn't a UX inconvenience; it's exposure severe enough to take the business offline.

And Consumer Lending wasn't transforming in isolation — multiple legacy systems, platforms, and operating models were being replaced at the same time:

Consumer Lending product platform
Legacy noncompliant platform
→
New proprietary compliant platform
MSR servicing platform
Legacy back-office systems
→
New MSR servicing platform
Design system
Dated legacy design system
→
New governed, accessible design system
Operating model
Business-led & “Wagile”
→
HCD + digital-first & SAFe Agile

The crisis

Three problems compounding at once

The vendor collapse

The platform strategy depended on a vendor that couldn't pass enterprise security and compliance review. Overnight, "configure a proven platform" became "build a new one from scratch" — in about nine months.

The regulatory clock

Under active regulatory exposure, unresolved issues carried penalties severe enough to take Consumer Lending offline. The deadline wasn't ambitious — it was existential.

The design blind spot

The org had never integrated design into delivery and assumed it could run parallel to development — not realizing design decisions are what dev builds from. Design got blamed as the bottleneck, and that fight burned nearly five of the nine months.

The reframe

Design isn't the blocker — it's the blueprint

"Design isn't the blocker; it's the blueprint the build depends on."

The turning point wasn't a screen — it was a sentence. I spent the early weeks putting out fires at the executive level, reframing the story from "design is slow" to what was actually true: the program had never scoped design in, and my team was doing backflips to make an impossible timeline work. Once leadership understood that design decisions drive development — that dev can't build what design hasn't defined — everything downstream became solvable.

How I led through it

Leading the work and doing the senior craft

As Design Director I led the digital lending-servicing pillar (Real Estate Lending, Consumer Lending, and Debt Recovery). For this Consumer Lending Phase 1, with no lead or senior designer on the team, I filled that role myself: I pulled institutional knowledge out of the org, defined and mapped the architecture with cross-functional leaders, then handed my two designers (mid-level and junior) the specifications they needed to build the screens — defining the workstream, reviewing and specifying every iteration, and approving the work.

  • Level-set and rebuilt trust. Partnered directly with my key stakeholder to establish trust and teach the team how design integrates into development and delivery — the missing piece that had put the program at risk.
  • Prioritized ruthlessly. Together we separated what was absolutely critical from what could be staggered and refreshed later. We aligned on six features for Phase 1.
  • Stair-stepped the delivery. Instead of a waterfall, I put the team on a rolling schedule where features delivered in staggered steps — keeping the team at full capacity from day one to the deadline, and de-risking the fixed timeline.

Same stair-stepped model, compressed from ~18 increments (typical) to ~12 (accelerated) — the animation loops between the two; hover to pause.

Operating principles

Rules that governed every decision

  • 01Design leads the build.

    Design decisions dictate development — so design goes first, as the blueprint.

  • 02Parity by default.

    Members and MSRs should see and do the same things; no more asymmetric tooling.

  • 03Kill the dead-ends.

    Every "please call us" is a design failure to move to self-service.

  • 04Accessible, on the system.

    Everything composed from our governed, accessible design system, to strict standards.

  • 05Automate away manual error.

    Replace hand-edits with automated, verifiable flows.

  • 06Ship in stair-steps.

    Rolling delivery keeps the team at capacity and de-risks a fixed deadline.

What shipped

Six features, all delivered

Cross-cutting wins: Member/MSR parity · visible status · fewer digital dead-ends · accessible componentry from our governed design system · automation that cut manual error and call volume.

1 · Payoff Quote

Gap: a digital dead-end (members had to call in), vague status, deprecated UI.  After: self-service Member/MSR parity, visible status, accessible components.  Future state: get more granular on payoff-quote type, guiding members to the right source pages.

2 · Payment Extension

Gap: the legacy flow indiscriminately routed members to call in — whether or not a call added value.  After: removed the dead-end; visible status and Member/MSR parity on accessible components.

3 · Loan History (MSR view)

Gap: legacy UI, unused options, confusing naming — and the legacy origination system did little for MSRs, with limits that bounded improvement.  After: a refined UI with more at-a-glance information, a clearer taxonomy, and functionality scoped for a future iteration.

4 · MSR Account Summary (new)

Gap: MSRs saw different information than members, and a different view per product — a disadvantage.  After: Member/MSR information parity plus a flexible display framework consistent across products (deposits, credit card, consumer loans).

5 · Back-Office Loan Adjustment Calculator (BLAC)

A back-office tool for processing rate mismatches, corrections, and remediations that update a loan's rate — directly tied to the regulatory fixes at stake.  Gap: manual edits straight to the system of record invited error; legacy UI.  Research: MSR interviews surfaced input fields no one used during rate corrections.  After: rebuilt on the new MSR platform — a streamlined workflow with fewer steps; selecting a loan auto-fills its details; unused fields converted to static data; a success CTA linking straight to the next step (verifying the member-letter details). Manual-error risk designed out.

6 · Automatic Payment Plan (APP)

The clearest proof of the new operating model paying off.  After: a consistent, cohesive cross-product experience (with Member/MSR parity) that lifts satisfaction (MSAT) and drives call reduction; we replaced heavier e-sign with a simpler electronic authorization, consistent with Payments — tightening consistency across the bank's digital ecosystem.  How it scaled: one team drove the base design while designers across Deposits, Credit Card, and Consumer Lending adapted it per product line — eliminating redundant work, cutting cost via out-of-the-box components, and freeing my team's capacity to keep Phase 1 moving.

Constraints

Working within reality

  • The clock: ~9 months on paper — but nearly five were lost to escalation, leaving ~3–4 months to design all six features from scratch, with no out-of-the-box shortcuts.
  • Regulatory exposure: active compliance/penalty pressure meant compliance and accessibility couldn't slip.
  • A stringently governed, highly accessible design system: everything had to compose from its components, to strict accessibility standards.
  • An org new to design: the partner team had never integrated design into delivery — I had to build the process and the trust while shipping.
  • Legacy systems: deprecated UI and a legacy system of record, plus a new MSR platform to build on.

Outcome

What shipped & what it changed

All six features shipped — designed on our stringently governed, highly accessible design system, and carried through: we stayed on to support our dev partners through full delivery and launch.

For members

  • Self-service where they used to have to call.
  • Clear, visible status.
  • Accessible experiences.

For MSRs

  • Information parity with members.
  • More at-a-glance context.
  • Automation that removed manual-error risk.
  • A consistent experience across products.

For the org

  • A multi-million-dollar Phase 1 shipped on deadline under regulatory pressure — in a ~3–4-month design window.
  • A repeatable design process and a Phase 2 roadmap.
  • Positioned to reduce calls and lift MSAT.

For the enterprise

  • A new cross-product operating model — one team drives base designs others adapt per product line.
  • Eliminated redundant work; cut cost via out-of-the-box components.
  • Improved shared-services scheduling across Deposits, Credit Card, and Consumer Lending.

In this environment, post-launch analytics weren't surfaced to design; outcomes reflect shipping all six features against a fixed deadline, stakeholder adoption of the new design process, and the roadmap it unlocked.

Retrospective

Phase 1 lessons

  • Design needs lead time — define the solution before the production process. Design is the blueprint the build depends on; it can't run concurrently.
  • The cost of an unknown process. Not understanding design's role hurt everyone — so it became the first thing I fixed.
  • Set expectations early. The single biggest lever was aligning everyone, up front, on how design actually works.
  • Teams norm by doing. Forming-storming-norming doesn't just happen — it happens because people are in it together, coming to know what they don't know.
  • Synchronicity is the unlock. The right partners in the right conversations at the right time made lock-step delivery possible.

What's next

Phase 2

  • Align the operating model. Leadership-level conversations to make the Digital Ops Model complement the existing Consumer Lending process — folding in Phase 1's lessons.
  • Kick off with a shared foundation. A Servicing + design all-hands to align the org on the design process before the work starts.
  • Discovery & planning. A design program proposal and detailed project plans.
  • A highly collaborative process. Research and workshopping built in from the start — so Phase 2 never repeats Phase 1's scramble.

Reflection

Why this is the work I care about

We shipped all six features — but the lasting work went beyond the screens. I changed how an organization understood design, turning it from the perceived blocker into the driver that made an impossible timeline possible under real regulatory stakes, and left behind a process and a roadmap so the next phase starts from strength instead of crisis. That's the work I care about most: staying close enough to the craft to make great work possible — and building the conditions in which it can happen.
